startup.name: Rational
startup.description: Rational is building an accounting firm with no human staff. AI employees handle client intake, bookkeeping and filing with the IRS, selling the service to businesses at a claimed 90 percent lower cost with 24/7 support. Two founders in San Francisco. Customers pay a service fee like a firm would, so revenue is services style with software margins if automation holds. No customers or traction are given.

yc_acceptance.basis: Starting rate about 1 percent (YC investor line, third party range 0.6 to 2 percent). Test setup: already accepted, reference only. Up for a bold, YC friendly full stack AI services idea in a huge market and a large painful cost gap. Down for a two person team, no stated traction and regulatory exposure. Net about 4 percent as a plain applicant.
yc_acceptance.why_it_fails: YC would most plausibly worry that tax and accounting are regulated and trust dependent, so a firm with no humans cannot sign returns or take liability, and that AI accounting is already crowded with funded companies such as Basis and Pilot. A two person team with no named customers or filed returns makes the claim of zero humans look like a slogan rather than a working service.

ladder.why_it_fails: It fails to raise a round above about 500K if investors doubt that a no human firm can be licensed, insured and trusted with filings, and prefer funded software competitors that sell to existing CPA firms such as Basis, which raised a 100M Series B in February 2026. Two founders with no named customers make the claim hard to test. Analogs like Combinely and Cranston sell to accountants, a safer wedge than replacing them.

ladder.why_it_fails: A Series C requires a business of national scale, which means winning many clients across states and clearing licensing and insurance in each. Competition from Basis, Pilot and Rillet style products and the big firms makes the final scale up uncertain; most accounting companies in the cohort stop earlier.

outcomes.why_it_fails: The most likely failure is that the service never reaches reliable accuracy and legal standing without humans, so it must hire accountants and becomes a normal firm with lower margins, or customers churn after one tax season. Several AI accounting entrants hold the same positioning and larger funded rivals sell software to firms. Pivoting to a tool for accountants is the common escape path.

killers.risk: Regulation and liability: only licensed people can sign or represent clients before the IRS
killers.evidence: Filing returns and representing clients are regulated activities, so a firm with no humans needs licensed signers and insurance.
killers.mitigation: Partner with or hire a small licensed staff and keep AI as the production engine, not the legal signer.

killers.risk: Accuracy and trust: errors in books or filings cost customers real money
killers.evidence: Small business owners will not move filings to an unproven firm; Fondo took years to reach funding after building a human backed service.
killers.mitigation: Start with narrow work like bookkeeping for startups and publish error rates.

killers.risk: Funded AI accounting competitors sell to the firms instead and outspend
killers.evidence: Basis raised a 100M Series B in February 2026 to sell AI agents to accounting firms, and Pilot already serves startups.
killers.mitigation: Pick one niche such as tax for one business type where full automation is achievable.

killers.risk: Seasonal revenue and customer acquisition cost make unit economics weak
killers.evidence: Tax work concentrates in a few months and small businesses churn often, which raises acquisition cost.
killers.mitigation: Sell year round bookkeeping and annual contracts.

technical_complexity.rationale: Language models can do much of bookkeeping and form preparation, but reliable end to end work across messy documents, bank feeds and IRS e-filing needs many integrations and error checks. A two person team can build a demo in three months but not a trusted, audited system.

who: Basis and other AI accounting vendors
Large accounting firms building internal agents
takeover_risk.rationale: Funded AI accounting startups and incumbents like Intuit already ship agents, and large firms can adopt them. The zero human firm is a business model that a tool vendor cannot copy, but the underlying automation is replicable within about a year.

evidence.claim: AI accounting attracted large rounds in 2026, such as a 100M Series B for a vendor selling agents to accounting firms, showing strong buyer interest.
Market maps list many funded AI accounting startups, showing real spend on automation.

roadmap.goal: Prove one narrow service works with no human touching the work.
actions: Pick a single client type such as small startups and process their books end to end.
Resolve who legally signs filings with a licensed partner.
roadmap.proof: Ten paying clients with books closed by the AI alone.

roadmap.goal: Show revenue and low error rates to justify a round above 500K.
actions: Publish an error rate and human review rate for closed books.
Reach monthly revenue from recurring contracts.
roadmap.proof: Recurring monthly revenue and under 1 percent corrections.

roadmap.goal: Survive a full tax season at scale.
actions: File several hundred returns with automated checks and audit support.
Add a second client segment and hire a head of compliance.
roadmap.proof: Net retention above 90 percent after a tax season and gross margin above 60 percent.

roadmap.goal: Become a recognized national AI native firm.
actions: Expand state coverage, insurance and audit services.
Build referral channels with banks and software vendors.
roadmap.proof: Revenue growth above 2x with stable margins.

pros.point: Huge, boring market with a large cost gap
pros.evidence: Accounting is a large professional services spend, and AI accounting startups raised large rounds in 2026.

pros.evidence: Selling the service instead of a tool captures service revenue and gives data on every filing.

brand.name: Rational
brand.name_check: python3 -I scripts/name_features.py --score "Rational" --era 2022+: 8 characters, 3 syllables, kind invented_or_proper, a real word.
strengths: Short real word that suggests logic and trust for finance
weaknesses: Common word that is hard to own in search and shared with a well known software brand
brand.rationale: A short real word with a credible tone suits a finance firm, like past YC names such as Brex or Gusto that were simple and memorable. The shared meaning and an older software brand dilute it, so the effect on success is neutral.

narrative.headline: A bold zero human accounting firm in a hot category; likely to raise a seed but faces regulatory and accuracy hurdles at Series A.
narrative.general_summary: Rational sells accounting as a service done by AI agents, which captures the full fee in a large market and fits the full stack AI services theme investors liked in 2026. The team is two founders with no stated traction, and tax and accounting require licensed signers, trust and accuracy, so the main question is whether the work can really be done without people. AI accounting is crowded with funded companies, and the closest YC analogs raised seeds of a few million and grew slowly. We rate the seed as likely and the Series A below the cohort anchor because of regulatory and seasonal friction. Data is thin on the company itself.

assumptions: Seed means a round above about 500K within about 12 months of the batch start.
Only the YC input description was used; no traction is known.
Base rates are B2B 2022 to 2025 cohort numbers; recent batches are right censored.
Funding coverage in the knowledge base is partial, so known only rates are biased low.
Search results dated after 2026-07-06 were ignored.
